concepts.title: Ideal
concepts.inline: An ideal of a commutative ring \(R\) is an additive subgroup \(\mathfrak{a} \subseteq R\) closed under multiplication by arbitrary elements of \(R\). Ideals are precisely the kernels of ring homomorphisms and the subsets by which one can form quotient rings.

blocks.label: Motivation
blocks.body: Subrings are too rigid to support a good quotient construction: the image of a subring under a ring homomorphism need not allow the source to factor through. Ideals isolate exactly the subsets \(\mathfrak{a} \subseteq R\) for which the additive quotient \(R/\mathfrak{a}\) inherits a well-defined ring structure, and they correspond bijectively to kernels of ring homomorphisms out of \(R\). They are therefore the fundamental tool for studying congruences, divisibility, and geometric structure on \(\mathrm{Spec}(R)\).

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.body:
Let \(R\) be a commutative ring. An ideal of \(R\) is a subset \(\mathfrak{a} \subseteq R\) satisfying:
(i) \(0 \in \mathfrak{a}\);
(ii) if \(a, b \in \mathfrak{a}\) then \(a + b \in \mathfrak{a}\);
(iii) if \(a \in \mathfrak{a}\) and \(r \in R\) then \(ra \in \mathfrak{a}\).

blocks.label: Equivalent Characterizations
items: A subset \(\mathfrak{a} \subseteq R\) is an ideal if and only if it is the kernel \(\ker(\varphi)\) of some ring homomorphism \(\varphi : R \to S\).
A subset \(\mathfrak{a} \subseteq R\) is an ideal if and only if it is an \(R\)-submodule of \(R\) regarded as a module over itself.

A subset \(\mathfrak{a} \subseteq R\) is an ideal if and only if the relation \(a \sim b \iff a - b \in \mathfrak{a}\) is a congruence on \(R\), i.e.\ an equivalence relation compatible with both addition and multiplication.
blocks.proof:
Suppose \(\mathfrak{a}\) is an ideal in the sense of the definition. Define \(\varphi : R \to R/\mathfrak{a}\) as the canonical projection sending \(r\) to its coset \(r + \mathfrak{a}\); the axioms (i)–(iii) ensure that addition and multiplication on cosets are well defined and that \(\varphi\) is a ring homomorphism with kernel exactly \(\mathfrak{a}\). Conversely, if \(\mathfrak{a} = \ker(\varphi)\) for some ring homomorphism \(\varphi : R \to S\), then \(\varphi(0) = 0\) gives \(0 \in \mathfrak{a}\); if \(\varphi(a) = \varphi(b) = 0\) then \(\varphi(a+b) = 0\); and for any \(r \in R\), \(\varphi(ra) = \varphi(r)\varphi(a) = 0\), so \(\mathfrak{a}\) satisfies (i)–(iii).

The equivalence with the submodule characterization is immediate: the \(R\)-module axioms for a subset of \(R\) viewed as a module over itself read precisely as (i)–(iii).

Finally, suppose \(\mathfrak{a}\) is an ideal and define \(a \sim b\) by \(a - b \in \mathfrak{a}\). Reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity follow from (i), (iii) with \(r = -1\), and (ii) respectively. If \(a \sim a'\) and \(b \sim b'\), then \((a+b) - (a'+b') = (a-a') + (b-b') \in \mathfrak{a}\) by (ii), and \(ab - a'b' = a(b - b') + b'(a - a') \in \mathfrak{a}\) by (iii) and (ii), so \(\sim\) is a ring congruence. Conversely, given such a congruence, the equivalence class \(\mathfrak{a}\) of \(0\) is closed under addition by compatibility with \(+\), contains \(0\) by reflexivity, and is absorbing under multiplication because \(a \sim 0\) implies \(ra \sim r \cdot 0 = 0\), recovering (i)–(iii).

blocks.label: Proposition
blocks.body: The ideals of \(R\) form a complete lattice under inclusion. Arbitrary intersections of ideals are ideals; for any subset \(S \subseteq R\) there is a smallest ideal \((S)\) containing \(S\), consisting of all finite sums \(\sum_{i} r_i s_i\) with \(r_i \in R\) and \(s_i \in S\). The whole ring \(R\) is an ideal, called the unit ideal, and an ideal \(\mathfrak{a}\) equals \(R\) if and only if it contains a unit.
blocks.proof:
Let \(\{\mathfrak{a}_\lambda\}_{\lambda \in \Lambda}\) be a family of ideals and set \(\mathfrak{a} = \bigcap_\lambda \mathfrak{a}_\lambda\). Then \(0 \in \mathfrak{a}\); if \(a, b \in \mathfrak{a}\) then \(a + b \in \mathfrak{a}_\lambda\) for every \(\lambda\), so \(a + b \in \mathfrak{a}\); and similarly \(ra \in \mathfrak{a}\) for \(r \in R\). Thus \(\mathfrak{a}\) is an ideal, and the ideals form a complete lattice with meet given by intersection and join by the intersection of all ideals containing the union.

Given \(S \subseteq R\), let \(I = \{\sum_{i=1}^n r_i s_i : n \geq 0,\ r_i \in R,\ s_i \in S\}\), with the empty sum interpreted as \(0\). Then \(0 \in I\); sums of two such expressions are again of this form; and for \(r \in R\), \(r \cdot \sum_i r_i s_i = \sum_i (r r_i) s_i \in I\). Hence \(I\) is an ideal containing \(S\). Conversely, any ideal containing \(S\) must contain each \(r_i s_i\) by absorption and hence each finite sum by closure under addition, so \(I\) is the smallest such ideal, namely the intersection of all ideals containing \(S\).

Clearly \(R\) itself satisfies (i)–(iii). If \(\mathfrak{a}\) contains a unit \(u\), then for every \(r \in R\), \(r = r u^{-1} \cdot u \in \mathfrak{a}\) by absorption, so \(\mathfrak{a} = R\). Conversely, if \(\mathfrak{a} = R\) then \(1 \in \mathfrak{a}\), and \(1\) is a unit.

blocks.label: Examples
items: In \(\mathbb{Z}\), every ideal is principal of the form \(n\mathbb{Z}\) for some \(n \geq 0\); the lattice of ideals is the divisibility lattice in reverse.
In any ring \(R\), the zero ideal \((0) = \{0\}\) and the unit ideal \(R\) are always ideals; they coincide precisely when \(R\) is the zero ring.
If \(R\) is a field, the only ideals are \((0)\) and \(R\), since any nonzero element is a unit.
The kernel of the evaluation map \(k[x] \to k\), \(f \mapsto f(0)\), is the ideal \((x)\), which is maximal because the quotient is the field \(k\).
In \(R = k[x,y]\), the ideal \((x,y) = \{xf + yg : f, g \in R\}\) is not principal, illustrating that the smallest ideal containing a set generally requires sums.

concepts.title: Commutative Ring
concepts.inline: A commutative ring is a set \(R\) equipped with two binary operations, addition and multiplication, satisfying the usual abelian group axioms for addition, associativity and commutativity of multiplication, distributivity, and the existence of a multiplicative identity \(1\).

blocks.label: Motivation
blocks.body: Commutative rings are the central objects of commutative algebra and the algebraic foundation of algebraic geometry and algebraic number theory. They abstract the arithmetic of the integers \(\mathbb{Z}\) and of polynomial rings \(k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), capturing precisely the structure needed to study divisibility, congruences, varieties, and schemes. The commutativity axiom forces multiplication to behave like that of numbers or functions, allowing the development of a rich theory of ideals, prime ideals, localization, and spectra.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.body:
A commutative ring is a triple \((R,+,\cdot)\) consisting of a set \(R\) together with two binary operations \(+\colon R\times R\to R\) and \(\cdot\colon R\times R\to R\) satisfying the following axioms:
(i) \((R,+)\) is an abelian group, with identity element \(0\) and inverses denoted \(-a\);
(ii) multiplication is associative: \((ab)c = a(bc)\) for all \(a,b,c\in R\);
(iii) multiplication is commutative: \(ab = ba\) for all \(a,b\in R\);
(iv) there exists a multiplicative identity \(1\in R\) such that \(1\cdot a = a\) for all \(a\in R\);
(v) multiplication distributes over addition: \(a(b+c) = ab + ac\) for all \(a,b,c\in R\).

blocks.label: Proposition
blocks.body:
In any commutative ring \(R\), the following identities hold for all \(a,b\in R\):
(i) \(0\cdot a = 0\);
(ii) \((-a)b = -(ab) = a(-b)\);
(iii) \((-a)(-b) = ab\);
(iv) the multiplicative identity \(1\) is unique;
(v) if \(1 = 0\), then \(R = \{0\}\) is the zero ring.
blocks.proof: For (i), distributivity gives \(0\cdot a = (0+0)\cdot a = 0\cdot a + 0\cdot a\); subtracting \(0\cdot a\) from both sides in the abelian group \((R,+)\) yields \(0\cdot a = 0\). For (ii), we compute \(ab + (-a)b = (a + (-a))b = 0\cdot b = 0\) by (i), so \((-a)b\) is the additive inverse of \(ab\), i.e. \((-a)b = -(ab)\); the identity \(a(-b) = -(ab)\) follows symmetrically. For (iii), applying (ii) twice gives \((-a)(-b) = -(a(-b)) = -(-(ab)) = ab\). For (iv), if \(1\) and \(1'\) are both multiplicative identities, then \(1 = 1\cdot 1' = 1'\). For (v), if \(1 = 0\), then for every \(a\in R\) we have \(a = 1\cdot a = 0\cdot a = 0\) by (i), so \(R = \{0\}\).

blocks.label: Examples
items: The ring of integers \(\mathbb{Z}\) is the prototypical commutative ring; in fact it is the initial object in the category of commutative rings.
Any field \(k\), such as \(\mathbb{Q}\), \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\mathbb{C}\), or \(\mathbb{F}_p\), is a commutative ring in which every nonzero element is a unit.
The polynomial ring \(k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) over a field \(k\) is a commutative ring; its geometry is studied via its spectrum.
For any ideal \(\mathfrak{a}\subseteq R\), the quotient \(R/\mathfrak{a}\) is a commutative ring.
The zero ring \(\{0\}\), characterised by \(1 = 0\), is the terminal object in the category of commutative rings.

concepts.title: Ring Homomorphism
concepts.inline: A ring homomorphism is a map between rings that preserves addition, multiplication, and the multiplicative identity. It is the structure-preserving notion of morphism in the category of (commutative) rings.

blocks.label: Motivation
blocks.body: To compare rings and transport algebraic information between them, one needs maps that respect the entire ring structure. Ring homomorphisms make the collection of rings into a category, allow one to define kernels and images as ideals and subrings, and underlie virtually every construction in commutative algebra: quotient rings, localizations, polynomial extensions, evaluation maps, and the functor \(\mathrm{Spec}\) all arise from or produce ring homomorphisms.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.body:
Let \(R\) and \(S\) be commutative rings with identity. A ring homomorphism \(\varphi: R \to S\) is a function satisfying
(i) \(\varphi(a + b) = \varphi(a) + \varphi(b)\) for all \(a, b \in R\),
(ii) \(\varphi(ab) = \varphi(a)\varphi(b)\) for all \(a, b \in R\),
(iii) \(\varphi(1_R) = 1_S\).

blocks.label: Equivalent Characterizations
items: A function \(\varphi: R \to S\) is a ring homomorphism if and only if it is a homomorphism of additive abelian groups that is also multiplicative and sends \(1_R\) to \(1_S\).

A function \(\varphi: R \to S\) is a ring homomorphism if and only if its graph \(\{(r, \varphi(r)) : r \in R\} \subseteq R \times S\) is a subring of the product ring projecting isomorphically onto \(R\).

blocks.label: Proposition
blocks.body: Let \(\varphi: R \to S\) be a ring homomorphism. Then \(\ker(\varphi) := \varphi^{-1}(0)\) is an ideal of \(R\), the image \(\varphi(R)\) is a subring of \(S\), and \(\varphi\) factors as the composition of the canonical surjection \(R \twoheadrightarrow R/\ker(\varphi)\) followed by an injective ring homomorphism \(R/\ker(\varphi) \hookrightarrow S\) with image \(\varphi(R)\). In particular \(R/\ker(\varphi) \cong \varphi(R)\).
blocks.proof:
Write \(I = \ker(\varphi)\). For \(a, b \in I\) we have \(\varphi(a - b) = \varphi(a) - \varphi(b) = 0\), so \(I\) is an additive subgroup of \(R\). For \(a \in I\) and \(r \in R\), \(\varphi(ra) = \varphi(r)\varphi(a) = \varphi(r) \cdot 0 = 0\), so \(ra \in I\); thus \(I\) is an ideal.

The image \(\varphi(R)\) contains \(\varphi(1_R) = 1_S\), and for \(\varphi(a), \varphi(b) \in \varphi(R)\) one has \(\varphi(a) - \varphi(b) = \varphi(a-b) \in \varphi(R)\) and \(\varphi(a)\varphi(b) = \varphi(ab) \in \varphi(R)\), so \(\varphi(R)\) is a subring of \(S\).

Define \(\bar\varphi : R/I \to S\) by \(\bar\varphi(r + I) = \varphi(r)\). This is well-defined: if \(r + I = r' + I\), then \(r - r' \in I\), so \(\varphi(r) - \varphi(r') = \varphi(r - r') = 0\). It is a ring homomorphism because
\[
\bar\varphi((r+I)(s+I)) = \bar\varphi(rs + I) = \varphi(rs) = \varphi(r)\varphi(s) = \bar\varphi(r+I)\bar\varphi(s+I),
\]
and similarly for addition, and \(\bar\varphi(1 + I) = \varphi(1) = 1\). If \(\bar\varphi(r + I) = 0\), then \(\varphi(r) = 0\), so \(r \in I\) and \(r + I = 0\); hence \(\bar\varphi\) is injective. By construction \(\bar\varphi\) has image \(\varphi(R)\) and \(\varphi = \bar\varphi \circ \pi\) where \(\pi : R \to R/I\) is the canonical surjection. The corestriction \(R/I \to \varphi(R)\) of \(\bar\varphi\) is therefore a bijective ring homomorphism, hence a ring isomorphism.

blocks.label: Examples
items: For any commutative ring \(R\), the unique map \(\mathbb{Z} \to R\) sending \(1 \mapsto 1_R\) is a ring homomorphism; this exhibits \(\mathbb{Z}\) as the initial object of the category of commutative rings.
The reduction map \(\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\), \(a \mapsto a \bmod n\), is a surjective ring homomorphism with kernel \((n)\).
For a commutative ring \(R\) and an element \(s \in R\), the evaluation map \(\mathrm{ev}_s : R[x] \to R\), \(f \mapsto f(s)\), is a ring homomorphism whose kernel is the principal ideal \((x - s)\).

The inclusion \(\mathbb{Z} \hookrightarrow \mathbb{Q}\) is an injective ring homomorphism, but the additive map \(\mathbb{Z} \to \mathbb{Z}\), \(a \mapsto 2a\), is not a ring homomorphism since it fails to send \(1\) to \(1\).

concepts.title: quotient rings
concepts.inline: The quotient ring \(R/\mathfrak{a}\) is the ring of cosets of an ideal \(\mathfrak{a}\) in \(R\).

concepts.title: spectrum of a ring
concepts.inline: The spectrum \(\mathrm{Spec}(R)\) of a ring \(R\) is the set of prime ideals of \(R\), equipped with the Zariski topology.

concepts.title: maximal
concepts.inline: A maximal ideal of a ring \(R\) is a proper ideal not contained in any other proper ideal.

concepts.title: Prime Ideal
concepts.inline: A prime ideal of a commutative ring \(R\) is a proper ideal \(\mathfrak{p}\subsetneq R\) such that whenever \(ab\in\mathfrak{p}\), either \(a\in\mathfrak{p}\) or \(b\in\mathfrak{p}\). Equivalently, the quotient \(R/\mathfrak{p}\) is an integral domain.

blocks.label: Motivation
blocks.body: Prime ideals generalise prime numbers from \(\mathbb{Z}\) and provide the right setting for studying factorisation, divisibility, and localisation in arbitrary commutative rings. They are the points of the geometric object \(\mathrm{Spec}(R)\), so the entire dictionary between algebra and geometry — irreducible subvarieties, generic points, dimension — is phrased in terms of primes. Their behaviour under quotients and localisations, together with the fact that the complement of a prime is closed under multiplication, makes them the universal tool for reducing problems in \(R\) to problems in domains or local rings.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.body:
Let \(R\) be a commutative ring. An ideal \(\mathfrak{p}\subseteq R\) is called a prime ideal if \(\mathfrak{p}\neq R\) and for all \(a,b\in R\),
\[ ab\in\mathfrak{p}\;\Longrightarrow\;a\in\mathfrak{p}\;\text{or}\;b\in\mathfrak{p}. \]

blocks.label: Equivalent Characterizations
items: The quotient ring \(R/\mathfrak{p}\) is an integral domain.
The set \(S=R\setminus\mathfrak{p}\) is a multiplicatively closed subset of \(R\) containing \(1\) and not containing \(0\).

Whenever \(\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b}\subseteq R\) are ideals with \(\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}\subseteq\mathfrak{p}\), one has \(\mathfrak{a}\subseteq\mathfrak{p}\) or \(\mathfrak{b}\subseteq\mathfrak{p}\).
The localisation \(R_{\mathfrak{p}}\) at \(\mathfrak{p}\) is a local ring with maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{p}R_{\mathfrak{p}}\).

blocks.label: Proposition
blocks.body: Let \(\varphi\colon R\to S\) be a ring homomorphism. If \(\mathfrak{q}\subseteq S\) is a prime ideal, then \(\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak{q})\subseteq R\) is a prime ideal. Consequently the map \(\mathrm{Spec}(S)\to\mathrm{Spec}(R)\) sending \(\mathfrak{q}\mapsto\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak{q})\) is well-defined.
blocks.proof: Set \(\mathfrak{p}=\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak{q})\). Since \(\varphi(1)=1 otin\mathfrak{q}\), we have \(1 otin\mathfrak{p}\), so \(\mathfrak{p} eq R\). Now suppose \(a,b\in R\) with \(ab\in\mathfrak{p}\). Then \(\varphi(ab)=\varphi(a)\varphi(b)\in\mathfrak{q}\), and since \(\mathfrak{q}\) is prime in \(S\), either \(\varphi(a)\in\mathfrak{q}\) or \(\varphi(b)\in\mathfrak{q}\). In the first case \(a\in\mathfrak{p}\); in the second, \(b\in\mathfrak{p}\). Hence \(\mathfrak{p}\) is prime. (Note: the image \(\varphi(\mathfrak{p})\) of a prime is in general not prime; this is why one pulls back rather than pushes forward.)

blocks.label: Examples
items: In \(\mathbb{Z}\), the prime ideals are exactly \((0)\) and \((p)\) for \(p\) a prime number; thus \(\mathrm{Spec}(\mathbb{Z})=\{(0)\}\cup\{(p):p\text{ prime}\}\).
Every maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{m}\) of \(R\) is prime, since \(R/\mathfrak{m}\) is a field and hence a domain.
If \(R\) is an integral domain then \((0)\) is a prime ideal.
In \(k[x_1,\dots,x_n]\) with \(k\) a field, the ideal generated by an irreducible polynomial is prime, corresponding to an irreducible hypersurface.
The nilradical of \(R\) equals the intersection of all prime ideals of \(R\), so \(R\) is reduced iff the prime ideals collectively detect every non-nilpotent element.

concepts.title: Unit
concepts.inline: A \emph{unit} in a commutative ring \(R\) is an element possessing a multiplicative inverse. The units of \(R\) form an abelian group \(R^\times\) under multiplication.

blocks.label: Motivation
blocks.body: Units are the invertible elements of a ring, and they govern much of its arithmetic structure. Identifying which elements are units distinguishes fields (where every nonzero element is a unit) from more general rings, and the group of units \(R^\times\) is a fundamental invariant — for example, \(\mathbb{Z}^\times = \{\pm 1\}\), while \(K^\times\) for a field \(K\){ref:field} captures the entire multiplicative structure. The notion of unit is also dual to that of a non-unit, which is intimately related to maximal ideals and to localization{ref:localization-of-rings}.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.body: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring with multiplicative identity \(1\). An element \(u \in R\) is called a unit if there exists \(v \in R\) such that \(uv = 1\). The set of all units of \(R\) is denoted \(R^\times\) (or \(R^*\) or \(U(R)\)).

blocks.label: Equivalent Characterizations
items: The principal ideal generated by \(u\) is the whole ring: \((u) = R\).
The element \(u\) is not contained in any maximal ideal of \(R\).
The element \(u\) is not contained in any prime ideal of \(R\), provided \(R\) is nonzero.
The image of \(u\) in every quotient \(R/\mathfrak{m}\){ref:quotient-ring} by a maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{m}\) is nonzero.
blocks.proof:
Suppose \(u\) is a unit with inverse \(v\). Then \(1 = uv \in (u)\), so \((u) = R\). Conversely, if \((u) = R\), then \(1 \in (u)\), meaning \(1 = uv\) for some \(v \in R\), so \(u\) is a unit.

Now assume \(u\) is a unit. If \(\mathfrak{m}\) is any maximal (or more generally proper) ideal containing \(u\), then \(1 = uv \in \mathfrak{m}\), contradicting properness. Thus \(u\) lies in no maximal ideal. Conversely, if \(u\) is not a unit, then \((u) \subsetneq R\) is a proper ideal, hence is contained in some maximal ideal by Zorn's lemma, so \(u\) belongs to some maximal ideal. This proves the equivalence with the second characterization. The third is similar, noting that every maximal ideal is prime, and in a nonzero ring proper ideals are contained in maximal (hence prime) ideals.

Finally, \(u\) lies outside every maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{m}\) if and only if its image in \(R/\mathfrak{m}\) is nonzero for every \(\mathfrak{m}\), proving the last equivalence.

blocks.label: Proposition
blocks.body: For any commutative ring \(R\), the set \(R^\times\) of units forms an abelian group under the multiplication of \(R\), called the group of units of \(R\). Moreover, the inverse of a unit is unique.
blocks.proof:
We first show uniqueness of inverses. If \(u \in R\) and \(v, v' \in R\) both satisfy \(uv = 1\) and \(uv' = 1\), then by associativity and commutativity of multiplication,
\[ v = v \cdot 1 = v(uv') = (vu)v' = 1 \cdot v' = v'. \]
Hence each unit has a unique multiplicative inverse, which we denote \(u^{-1}\).

We now verify that \(R^\times\) is a group under multiplication. The element \(1\) is a unit since \(1 \cdot 1 = 1\), so \(1 \in R^\times\) provides an identity. If \(u, w \in R^\times\) with inverses \(u^{-1}, w^{-1}\), then
\[ (uw)(w^{-1}u^{-1}) = u(ww^{-1})u^{-1} = u \cdot 1 \cdot u^{-1} = uu^{-1} = 1, \]
so \(uw \in R^\times\) with inverse \(w^{-1}u^{-1}\); thus \(R^\times\) is closed under multiplication. If \(u \in R^\times\) with inverse \(u^{-1}\), then by definition \(u^{-1}\) is itself a unit with inverse \(u\), so \(R^\times\) is closed under taking inverses. Associativity of multiplication in \(R^\times\) is inherited from \(R\), and commutativity follows from commutativity of \(R\). Therefore \(R^\times\) is an abelian group.

blocks.label: Examples
items: In \(\mathbb{Z}\), the units are \(\mathbb{Z}^\times = \{+1, -1\}\).
In a field \(K\){ref:field}, every nonzero element is a unit: \(K^\times = K \setminus \{0\}\). Conversely, a nonzero commutative ring is a field if and only if every nonzero element is a unit.
In the polynomial ring \(K[x]\) over a field \(K\), the units are exactly the nonzero constants: \(K[x]^\times = K^\times\).
In \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\), the units are the residue classes \(\overline{a}\) with \(\gcd(a, n) = 1\); the group \((\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z})^\times\) has order \(\varphi(n)\).
In the formal power series ring \(K[\![x]\!]\), a series \(\sum a_n x^n\) is a unit if and only if its constant term \(a_0\) is a unit in \(K\).
If \(n \in R\) is nilpotent{ref:nilpotent-element}, then \(1 + n\) is a unit, with inverse \(1 - n + n^2 - n^3 + \cdots\) (a finite sum).

concepts.title: principal
concepts.inline: A principal ideal is an ideal generated by a single element.

concepts.title: field
concepts.inline: A field is a commutative ring in which every nonzero element is a unit.

concepts.title: Localization of Rings
concepts.inline: Given a commutative ring \(R\) and a multiplicatively closed subset \(S \subseteq R\), the localization \(S^{-1}R\) is a new ring in which every element of \(S\) becomes a unit. It is constructed as a ring of formal fractions \(r/s\) with \(r \in R\) and \(s \in S\), generalizing the passage from \(\mathbb{Z}\) to \(\mathbb{Q}\).

blocks.label: Motivation
blocks.body: Many properties of a ring are controlled by what happens near a prime ideal, or after inverting a particular set of elements. Localization provides a systematic way to invert a chosen family of elements while preserving as much algebraic structure as possible. It enables passage from global to local information, mirrors the geometric operation of restricting to an open subset of the spectrum, and is the algebraic counterpart of forming rings of rational functions defined away from a chosen zero locus.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.body:
Let \(R\) be a commutative ring and let \(S \subseteq R\) be a multiplicatively closed subset, meaning that \(1 \in S\) and \(s, t \in S\) implies \(st \in S\). Define a relation \(\sim\) on \(R \times S\) by
\[(r, s) \sim (r', s') \iff \exists\, u \in S \text{ such that } u(s'r - sr') = 0.\]
This is an equivalence relation; denote the class of \((r, s)\) by \(r/s\), and let \(S^{-1}R\) be the set of equivalence classes. Addition and multiplication are defined by
\[\frac{r}{s} + \frac{r'}{s'} := \frac{s'r + sr'}{ss'}, \qquad \frac{r}{s} \cdot \frac{r'}{s'} := \frac{rr'}{ss'},\]
with zero \(0/1\) and unit \(1/1\). These operations are well defined and turn \(S^{-1}R\) into a commutative ring, the localization of \(R\) at \(S\). The canonical map \(\iota \colon R \to S^{-1}R\), \(r \mapsto r/1\), is a ring homomorphism sending every \(s \in S\) to a unit.
blocks.proof:
We verify that \(\sim\) is an equivalence relation. Reflexivity and symmetry are immediate from the definition. For transitivity, suppose \((r,s) \sim (r',s')\) and \((r',s') \sim (r'',s'')\), so there exist \(u, v \in S\) with \(u(s'r - sr') = 0\) and \(v(s''r' - s'r'') = 0\). Multiplying the first equation by \(vs''\) and the second by \(us\) and adding,
\[uvs'(s''r - sr'') = uvs''(s'r - sr') + uvs(s''r' - s'r'') = 0.\]
Since \(uvs' \in S\), this shows \((r,s) \sim (r'',s'')\).

Next, we check that addition and multiplication are well defined. Suppose \(r/s = r_1/s_1\), witnessed by \(u(s_1 r - s r_1) = 0\) for some \(u \in S\). For multiplication by \(r'/s'\), we compute
\[u(s_1 s' \cdot rr' - s s' \cdot r_1 r') = u r' s'(s_1 r - s r_1) = 0,\]
so \(rr'/ss' = r_1 r'/s_1 s'\). For addition,
\[u\big(s_1 s'(s'r + sr') - ss'(s' r_1 + s_1 r')\big) \\ = u s'^2 (s_1 r - s r_1) = 0,\]
so \((s'r + sr')/(ss') = (s' r_1 + s_1 r')/(s_1 s')\). A symmetric argument handles the second coordinate. The ring axioms are then routinely inherited from \(R\): commutativity, associativity, and distributivity are straightforward, with \(0/1\) acting as the additive identity and \(1/1\) as the multiplicative identity.

Finally, \(\iota(r) = r/1\) preserves sums and products by definition, and for \(s \in S\) we have \((s/1)(1/s) = s/s = 1/1\), so \(\iota(s)\) is a unit in \(S^{-1}R\).

blocks.label: Equivalent Characterizations
items: Universal property: the pair \((S^{-1}R, \iota)\) is initial among ring homomorphisms \(\varphi \colon R \to T\) such that \(\varphi(s)\) is a unit in \(T\) for every \(s \in S\); that is, every such \(\varphi\) factors uniquely as \(\varphi = \tilde{\varphi} \circ \iota\) for a unique ring homomorphism \(\tilde{\varphi} \colon S^{-1}R \to T\).

Presentation by generators and relations: \(S^{-1}R\) is isomorphic to \(R[x_s : s \in S]/I\), where \(I\) is the ideal generated by all \(s x_s - 1\) for \(s \in S\), with \(\iota\) the composition \(R \hookrightarrow R[x_s : s \in S] \twoheadrightarrow R[x_s]/I\).
blocks.proof:
We prove that the explicit construction satisfies the universal property. Suppose \(\varphi \colon R \to T\) is a ring homomorphism with \(\varphi(s) \in T^\times\) for every \(s \in S\). Define \(\tilde{\varphi} \colon S^{-1}R \to T\) by \(\tilde{\varphi}(r/s) := \varphi(r)\varphi(s)^{-1}\). If \(r/s = r'/s'\), there exists \(u \in S\) with \(u(s'r - sr') = 0\); applying \(\varphi\) gives \(\varphi(u)(\varphi(s')\varphi(r) - \varphi(s)\varphi(r')) = 0\), and since \(\varphi(u)\) is a unit we deduce \(\varphi(r)\varphi(s)^{-1} = \varphi(r')\varphi(s')^{-1}\). Hence \(\tilde{\varphi}\) is well defined. A direct calculation confirms it is a ring homomorphism, and clearly \(\tilde{\varphi} \circ \iota = \varphi\). Uniqueness follows because any ring homomorphism \(\psi \colon S^{-1}R \to T\) extending \(\varphi\) must satisfy \(\psi(1/s) = \psi(s/1)^{-1} = \varphi(s)^{-1}\), forcing \(\psi(r/s) = \varphi(r)\varphi(s)^{-1}\).

For the presentation, let \(A := R[x_s : s \in S]/I\) with \(I = (sx_s - 1 : s \in S)\), and let \(\pi \colon R \to A\) be the natural map. In \(A\), each image \(\bar{s} = \pi(s)\) is a unit with inverse \(\bar{x}_s\). By the universal property just established, there is a unique homomorphism \(\Phi \colon S^{-1}R \to A\) with \(\Phi(r/1) = \pi(r)\) and necessarily \(\Phi(1/s) = \bar{x}_s\). Conversely, define \(\Psi \colon R[x_s : s \in S] \to S^{-1}R\) by sending \(r \mapsto r/1\) and \(x_s \mapsto 1/s\); then \(\Psi(sx_s - 1) = 0\), so \(\Psi\) factors through \(A\), giving \(\bar{\Psi} \colon A \to S^{-1}R\). The compositions \(\Phi \circ \bar{\Psi}\) and \(\bar{\Psi} \circ \Phi\) fix the generators on each side, hence are the identity, establishing the isomorphism.

blocks.label: Examples
items: Field of fractions: if \(R\) is an integral domain and \(S = R \setminus \{0\}\), then \(S^{-1}R\) is the field of fractions of \(R\); for \(R = \mathbb{Z}\) this recovers \(\mathbb{Q}\).

Localization at a prime: if \(\mathfrak{p}\) is a prime ideal of \(R\), then \(S = R \setminus \mathfrak{p}\) is multiplicatively closed, and \(R_\mathfrak{p} := S^{-1}R\) is a local ring with unique maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{p} R_\mathfrak{p}\).

Inverting a single element: for \(f \in R\) the set \(S = \{1, f, f^2, \ldots\}\) is multiplicatively closed, and \(R_f := S^{-1}R \cong R[x]/(fx - 1)\); geometrically this corresponds to restricting to the open subset \(D(f) \subseteq \mathrm{Spec}(R)\).
Trivial cases: if \(0 \in S\), then \(S^{-1}R = 0\) is the zero ring; if \(S\) consists entirely of units, then \(\iota \colon R \to S^{-1}R\) is already an isomorphism.

concepts.title: universal property
concepts.inline: A universal property characterizes an object up to unique isomorphism by a mapping property it satisfies among all objects of a given kind.

concepts.title: field of fractions
concepts.inline: The field of fractions of an integral domain \(R\) is the smallest field containing \(R\), formed as equivalence classes of fractions \(r/s\) with \(s \neq 0\).

concepts.title: Integral Domain
concepts.inline: An integral domain is a nonzero commutative ring in which the product of any two nonzero elements is nonzero. Equivalently, it is a commutative ring with no nontrivial zero divisors, allowing cancellation \(ab = ac \Rightarrow b = c\) whenever \(a \neq 0\).

blocks.label: Motivation
blocks.body: In \(\mathbb{Z}\) one freely cancels: if \(2x = 2y\), then \(x = y\). But in \(\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}\) the equation \(2 \cdot 1 = 2 \cdot 4\) holds even though \(1 \neq 4\), because \(2 \cdot 3 = 0\) without either factor being zero. This phenomenon — a product of nonzero elements collapsing to zero — wrecks the most basic algebraic manipulations and blocks any sensible notion of fractions: how can one form \(a/b\) when multiplying by \(b\) loses information? To single out the rings where polynomial identities behave as expected and where one can later embed into a field of quotients, we isolate exactly the rings in which this pathology is absent.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.body:
An integral domain is a commutative ring \(R\) such that
(i) \(R \neq 0\), i.e. \(1 \neq 0\) in \(R\);
(ii) for all \(a, b \in R\), if \(ab = 0\) then \(a = 0\) or \(b = 0\).

blocks.label: Equivalent Characterizations
items: \(R\) is a nonzero commutative ring in which the zero ideal \((0)\) is a prime ideal.
\(R\) is a nonzero commutative ring satisfying the cancellation law: for all \(a, b, c \in R\) with \(a \neq 0\), \(ab = ac\) implies \(b = c\).
\(R\) is a nonzero commutative ring that embeds as a subring of a field (namely its field of fractions).
blocks.proof:
Let \(R\) be a nonzero commutative ring. The condition that \((0)\) is prime states precisely that \(ab \in (0)\) implies \(a \in (0)\) or \(b \in (0)\), which is condition (ii) of the definition. Hence the first characterization is a direct restatement.

For the cancellation law, suppose \(R\) is an integral domain and \(ab = ac\) with \(a eq 0\). Then \(a(b-c) = 0\), so by the defining property \(b - c = 0\), i.e. \(b = c\). Conversely, if cancellation holds and \(ab = 0\) with \(a eq 0\), then \(ab = a \cdot 0\) gives \(b = 0\).

For the embedding into a field, if \(R\) is an integral domain then the set \(S = R \setminus \{0\}\) is multiplicatively closed (it contains \(1\) and is closed under products by the domain property), so the localization \(S^{-1}R\) is defined. Every nonzero element \(a/s\) has inverse \(s/a\), so \(S^{-1}R\) is a field, and the canonical map \(R o S^{-1}R\), \(r \mapsto r/1\), is injective precisely because \(r/1 = 0\) forces \(rt = 0\) for some \(t \in S\), hence \(r = 0\). Conversely, any subring of a field is itself a commutative ring in which \(ab = 0\) forces \(a = 0\) or \(b = 0\), since fields have no zero divisors, and a subring of a field is nonzero provided it contains \(1 eq 0\).

blocks.label: Proposition
blocks.body: A commutative ring \(R\) is an integral domain if and only if the polynomial ring \(R[x]\) is an integral domain. In that case, for nonzero \(f, g \in R[x]\) one has \(\deg(fg) = \deg(f) + \deg(g)\).
blocks.proof:
Suppose \(R\) is an integral domain. Since \(R \subseteq R[x]\) and \(1_{R[x]} = 1_R eq 0\), the ring \(R[x]\) is nonzero. Let \(f, g \in R[x]\) be nonzero, write
\[ f = a_m x^m + ext{lower terms}, \qquad g = b_n x^n + ext{lower terms}, \]
with \(a_m, b_n eq 0\) the leading coefficients. The coefficient of \(x^{m+n}\) in \(fg\) is \(a_m b_n\), which is nonzero because \(R\) is a domain. Hence \(fg eq 0\) and \(\deg(fg) = m + n = \deg(f) + \deg(g)\). This shows \(R[x]\) is an integral domain and establishes the degree formula.

Conversely, suppose \(R[x]\) is an integral domain. Then \(R[x] eq 0\) forces \(R eq 0\), and any zero divisor relation \(ab = 0\) in \(R\) is also a relation in \(R[x]\) (viewing \(a, b\) as constant polynomials), so \(a = 0\) or \(b = 0\). Hence \(R\) is an integral domain.

blocks.label: Examples
items: The ring \(\mathbb{Z}\) of integers is the prototypical integral domain; its field of fractions is \(\mathbb{Q}\).
Every field is an integral domain, since nonzero elements are units and units cannot be zero divisors.
For any field \(k\), the polynomial ring \(k[x_1, \dots, x_n]\) is an integral domain.
The ring \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\) is an integral domain if and only if \(n\) is prime; for instance \(\mathbb{Z}/6\mathbb{Z}\) is not, since \(2 \cdot 3 = 0\).
The ring \(\mathbb{Z}[i] = \{a + bi : a, b \in \mathbb{Z}\}\) of Gaussian integers is an integral domain, as a subring of \(\mathbb{C}\).
A quotient \(R/\mathfrak{p}\) is an integral domain if and only if \(\mathfrak{p}\) is a prime ideal of \(R\).

concepts.title: local ring
concepts.inline: A local ring is a commutative ring with a unique maximal ideal.

concepts.title: zero ring
concepts.inline: The zero ring is the ring with a single element in which \(0 = 1\).

concepts.title: Nilradical
concepts.inline: The nilradical \(\mathfrak{N}(R)\) of a commutative ring \(R\) is the set of all nilpotent elements of \(R\). It is an ideal, and equals the intersection of all prime ideals of \(R\).

blocks.label: Motivation
blocks.body: In commutative algebra one frequently wants to detect and discard nilpotent elements, because they vanish on the spectrum yet obstruct geometric intuition: a function whose square is zero is invisible to points but visible in the algebra. Collecting all such elements into a single ideal produces a canonical reduced quotient \(R/\mathfrak{N}(R)\), which has the same prime spectrum as \(R\) but no nonzero nilpotents. The nilradical thus mediates between the algebraic and geometric pictures, and its identification with the intersection of all prime ideals is one of the first nontrivial bridges of the theory.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.body:
Let \(R\) be a commutative ring. The nilradical of \(R\) is
\[
\mathfrak{N}(R) \;=\; \{\, x \in R : x^n = 0 \text{ for some integer } n \geq 1 \,\}.
\]
blocks.proof:
We verify that \(\mathfrak{N}(R)\) is an ideal of \(R\). Clearly \(0 \in \mathfrak{N}(R)\). Suppose \(x, y \in \mathfrak{N}(R)\) with \(x^m = 0\) and \(y^n = 0\). By the binomial theorem,
\[
(x+y)^{m+n-1} \;=\; \sum_{k=0}^{m+n-1} \binom{m+n-1}{k} x^k y^{m+n-1-k}.
\]
In each term either \(k \geq m\), so \(x^k = 0\), or \(m+n-1-k \geq n\), so \(y^{m+n-1-k} = 0\). Hence \((x+y)^{m+n-1} = 0\) and \(x+y \in \mathfrak{N}(R)\). For \(r \in R\) and \(x \in \mathfrak{N}(R)\) with \(x^m = 0\), commutativity gives \((rx)^m = r^m x^m = 0\), so \(rx \in \mathfrak{N}(R)\). Thus \(\mathfrak{N}(R)\) is an ideal.

blocks.label: Equivalent Characterizations
items: \(\mathfrak{N}(R) = \bigcap_{\mathfrak{p} \in \mathrm{Spec}(R)} \mathfrak{p}\), the intersection of all prime ideals of \(R\).
\(\mathfrak{N}(R)\) is the smallest ideal \(I \subseteq R\) such that the quotient \(R/I\) is reduced (i.e.\ has no nonzero nilpotent elements).
blocks.proof:
We prove \(\mathfrak{N}(R) = igcap_{\mathfrak{p}} \mathfrak{p}\), where the intersection ranges over all prime ideals of \(R\). For the inclusion \(\subseteq\), let \(x \in \mathfrak{N}(R)\), so \(x^n = 0\) for some \(n \geq 1\). For any prime \(\mathfrak{p}\), \(x^n = 0 \in \mathfrak{p}\), and primality forces \(x \in \mathfrak{p}\). Hence \(x\) lies in every prime ideal.

For the reverse inclusion, suppose \(x \in R\) is not nilpotent; we construct a prime ideal \(\mathfrak{p}\) avoiding \(x\). Consider the set
\[
\Sigma \;=\; \{\, I rianglelefteq R : x^n otin I ext{ for all } n \geq 1 \,\}.
\]
The zero ideal lies in \(\Sigma\) since \(x\) is not nilpotent, so \(\Sigma\) is nonempty. It is partially ordered by inclusion, and any chain \(\{I_\alpha\}\) in \(\Sigma\) has upper bound \( igcup_\alpha I_\alpha\), which still avoids every power of \(x\). By Zorn's lemma, \(\Sigma\) contains a maximal element \(\mathfrak{p}\). We claim \(\mathfrak{p}\) is prime. Suppose \(a, b otin \mathfrak{p}\); then by maximality of \(\mathfrak{p}\) in \(\Sigma\), both \(\mathfrak{p} + (a)\) and \(\mathfrak{p} + (b)\) fail to lie in \(\Sigma\), so there exist \(m, n \geq 1\) with
\[
x^m \in \mathfrak{p} + (a), \qquad x^n \in \mathfrak{p} + (b).
\]
Multiplying, \(x^{m+n} \in \mathfrak{p} + (ab)\). If \(ab \in \mathfrak{p}\) then \(x^{m+n} \in \mathfrak{p}\), contradicting \(\mathfrak{p} \in \Sigma\). Hence \(ab otin \mathfrak{p}\), proving primality. Since \(x otin \mathfrak{p}\), \(x\) does not lie in the intersection of all primes.

For the second equivalence, the quotient \(R/\mathfrak{N}(R)\) is reduced: if \( ar{x}^n = 0\) in \(R/\mathfrak{N}(R)\), then \(x^n \in \mathfrak{N}(R)\), so \((x^n)^m = 0\) for some \(m\), giving \(x \in \mathfrak{N}(R)\) and \( ar{x} = 0\). Conversely, if \(I \subseteq R\) is any ideal with \(R/I\) reduced, then for \(x \in \mathfrak{N}(R)\) with \(x^n = 0\), the image \( ar{x} \in R/I\) satisfies \( ar{x}^n = 0\), hence \( ar{x} = 0\), i.e.\ \(x \in I\). Thus \(\mathfrak{N}(R) \subseteq I\), making \(\mathfrak{N}(R)\) the smallest such ideal.

blocks.label: Proposition
blocks.body: The quotient \(R_{\mathrm{red}} := R/\mathfrak{N}(R)\) is a reduced ring, and the canonical projection \(R \to R_{\mathrm{red}}\) induces a homeomorphism \(\mathrm{Spec}(R_{\mathrm{red}}) \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathrm{Spec}(R)\).

blocks.label: Examples
items: In \(\mathbb{Z}\), and more generally in any integral domain, the only nilpotent element is \(0\), so \(\mathfrak{N}(R) = (0)\) and \(R\) is reduced.
In \(\mathbb{Z}/p^k\mathbb{Z}\) for \(k \geq 1\), the nilradical is the principal ideal \((p)\), since \(p^k = 0\) but no element outside \((p)\) is nilpotent.
In \(R = k[x]/(x^n)\) over a field \(k\), the nilradical is the maximal ideal \((\bar{x})\), and the reduced quotient is \(k\).

In \(\mathbb{Z}/12\mathbb{Z}\), the nilpotents are \(\{0, 6\}\), since \(6^2 = 36 \equiv 0\); the nilradical is \((6)\), consistent with the prime factorization \(12 = 2^2 \cdot 3\) and the intersection \((2) \cap (3) = (6)\).

concepts.title: Nilpotent Element
concepts.inline: A nilpotent element of a commutative ring \(R\) is an element \(x \in R\) such that \(x^n = 0\) for some positive integer \(n\). The set of all such elements forms the nilradical of \(R\).

blocks.label: Motivation
blocks.body: Nilpotent elements measure the failure of a ring to be reduced: they are the "infinitesimal" elements that vanish under some power. Their presence reflects non-trivial scheme-theoretic structure in algebraic geometry, where nilpotents encode infinitesimal thickenings, and their absence characterizes reduced rings. Controlling nilpotents is essential to understanding the difference between a ring and its associated topological space \(\mathrm{Spec}(R)\), since nilpotents lie in every prime ideal yet may be non-zero.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.body: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring. An element \(x \in R\) is called nilpotent if there exists a positive integer \(n \geq 1\) such that \(x^n = 0\) in \(R\). The smallest such \(n\) is called the nilpotency index of \(x\).

blocks.label: Equivalent Characterizations
items: The element \(x\) lies in the nilradical \(\mathfrak{N}(R) = \bigcap_{\mathfrak{p} \in \mathrm{Spec}(R)} \mathfrak{p}\), i.e.\ \(x\) belongs to every prime ideal of \(R\).
The image of \(x\) in every integral domain quotient \(R/\mathfrak{p}\) is zero, for every prime ideal \(\mathfrak{p}\).
The localization \(R[x^{-1}] = R_x\) is the zero ring.
blocks.proof:
Suppose \(x^n = 0\) for some \(n \geq 1\). For any prime ideal \(\mathfrak{p}\), we have \(x^n = 0 \in \mathfrak{p}\), and primality forces \(x \in \mathfrak{p}\). Thus \(x\) lies in the intersection of all primes, which by definition is the nilradical. Conversely, suppose \(x \in \mathfrak{N}(R)\); we show \(x\) is nilpotent. If \(x\) were not nilpotent, then the multiplicatively closed set \(S = \{1, x, x^2, \ldots\}\) would not contain \(0\), so the localization \(R_x = S^{-1}R\) would be non-zero. By a standard application of Zorn's lemma, \(R_x\) contains a maximal ideal, and its contraction along the localization map \(R \to R_x\) would be a prime ideal of \(R\) disjoint from \(S\), hence not containing \(x\), contradicting \(x \in \mathfrak{N}(R)\).

The equivalence with the second condition is immediate: \(x \in \mathfrak{p}\) if and only if the image of \(x\) in \(R/\mathfrak{p}\) is zero. For the third, observe that \(R_x = 0\) if and only if \(1 = 0\) in \(R_x\), which holds if and only if \(x^n \cdot 1 = x^n \cdot 0 = 0\) in \(R\) for some \(n \geq 0\), i.e.\ \(x^n = 0\).

blocks.label: Proposition
blocks.body: The set \(\mathfrak{N}(R)\) of nilpotent elements of a commutative ring \(R\) is an ideal of \(R\), and the quotient \(R/\mathfrak{N}(R)\) is a reduced ring, i.e.\ contains no non-zero nilpotents.
blocks.proof:
We show \(\mathfrak{N}(R)\) is closed under addition and absorbs multiplication by \(R\). Clearly \(0 \in \mathfrak{N}(R)\). If \(x, y \in \mathfrak{N}(R)\) with \(x^m = 0\) and \(y^n = 0\), then by the binomial theorem (valid since \(R\) is commutative),
\[(x+y)^{m+n-1} = \sum_{k=0}^{m+n-1} \binom{m+n-1}{k} x^k y^{m+n-1-k}.\]
In each term, either \(k \geq m\), so \(x^k = 0\), or \(m+n-1-k \geq n\), so \(y^{m+n-1-k} = 0\). Hence every term vanishes, and \((x+y)^{m+n-1} = 0\), showing \(x+y \in \mathfrak{N}(R)\). For absorption, if \(r \in R\) and \(x^m = 0\), then \((rx)^m = r^m x^m = 0\), so \(rx \in \mathfrak{N}(R)\). Thus \(\mathfrak{N}(R)\) is an ideal.

For the second claim, suppose \(\bar{x} \in R/\mathfrak{N}(R)\) satisfies \(\bar{x}^n = 0\), i.e.\ \(x^n \in \mathfrak{N}(R)\). Then \((x^n)^k = x^{nk} = 0\) for some \(k \geq 1\), so \(x \in \mathfrak{N}(R)\), whence \(\bar{x} = 0\). Therefore \(R/\mathfrak{N}(R)\) is reduced.

blocks.label: Examples
items: In \(\mathbb{Z}\), the only nilpotent element is \(0\), since \(\mathbb{Z}\) is an integral domain.
In \(\mathbb{Z}/p^k\mathbb{Z}\), the element \(p\) is nilpotent with nilpotency index \(k\); more generally, the nilpotents are the multiples of \(p\).
In \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\) with \(n = p_1^{e_1} \cdots p_r^{e_r}\), the nilpotent elements are the multiples of the radical \(p_1 \cdots p_r\).
In any integral domain, and in particular in any field, the only nilpotent element is \(0\).
In the polynomial ring \(R[t]/(t^n)\), the class of \(t\) is nilpotent of index exactly \(n\). This ring models infinitesimal thickenings of a point in algebraic geometry.

concepts.title: commutative algebra
concepts.inline: Commutative algebra is the branch of algebra studying commutative rings, their ideals, and modules over them.

concepts.title: reduced
concepts.inline: A ring is reduced if it has no nonzero nilpotent elements.

concepts.title: additive subgroup
concepts.inline: An additive subgroup of a ring is a subset closed under addition and negation containing 0.

concepts.title: Subrings
concepts.inline: A subring is a subset of a ring that is closed under the ring operations and contains the identity.

concepts.title: kernel
concepts.inline: The kernel of a ring homomorphism \(\varphi : R \to S\) is the preimage \(\varphi^{-1}(0)\) of zero.

concepts.title: module
concepts.inline: A module over a ring \(R\) is an abelian group equipped with a compatible scalar multiplication by \(R\).

concepts.title: equivalence relation
concepts.inline: An equivalence relation is a binary relation that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive.

concepts.title: complete lattice
concepts.inline: A complete lattice is a partially ordered set in which every subset has a supremum and an infimum.
Localisation is the construction of a ring \(S^{-1}R\) by formally inverting a multiplicatively closed subset \(S\subseteq R\).
Localisations are rings obtained from \(R\) by formally inverting elements of a multiplicatively closed subset.

concepts.title: multiplicatively closed subset
concepts.inline: A multiplicatively closed subset of a ring \(R\) is a subset \(S\subseteq R\) containing \(1\) and closed under multiplication.

concepts.title: irreducible polynomial
concepts.inline: An irreducible polynomial is a non-constant polynomial that cannot be factored as a product of two non-constant polynomials.

concepts.title: Abelian Group
concepts.inline: An \emph{abelian group} is a group whose binary operation is commutative. Equivalently, it is a set \(A\) equipped with an associative, commutative addition \(+\) admitting an identity \(0\) and additive inverses.

blocks.label: Motivation
blocks.body: Abelian groups form the additive backbone of every commutative ring: the underlying additive structure of a ring, the structure of every ideal, and the structure of every module are all abelian groups. Isolating the commutative-additive axioms cleanly separates the additive theory from the multiplicative structure, and provides the natural target for homomorphisms whenever order of operations does not matter. Historically, the study of abelian groups grew out of number theory (classes of quadratic forms, ideal class groups) and underpins homological algebra, where the category of abelian groups is the prototypical abelian category.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.body:
An abelian group is a pair \((A,+)\) consisting of a set \(A\) and a binary operation \(+ : A \times A \to A\) satisfying:
(i) (associativity) \((a+b)+c = a+(b+c)\) for all \(a,b,c \in A\);
(ii) (identity) there exists \(0 \in A\) such that \(a + 0 = a\) for all \(a \in A\);
(iii) (inverses) for every \(a \in A\) there exists \(-a \in A\) such that \(a + (-a) = 0\);
(iv) (commutativity) \(a + b = b + a\) for all \(a, b \in A\).

blocks.label: Equivalent Characterizations
items: A \(\mathbb{Z}\)-module: an abelian group is exactly a module over the ring \(\mathbb{Z}\), with scalar action \(n \cdot a\) given by repeated addition.
A group object in the category of sets whose multiplication map factors through the symmetric quotient, i.e.\ a group \((G,\cdot)\) satisfying \(g \cdot h = h \cdot g\) for all \(g,h \in G\).

blocks.label: Examples
items: The integers \((\mathbb{Z},+)\), the prototypical infinite cyclic abelian group.
For any commutative ring \(R\), the underlying additive structure \((R,+)\) is an abelian group, as is every ideal \(\mathfrak{a} \subseteq R\).
The cyclic groups \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\) for \(n \geq 1\), and more generally any quotient \(A/B\) of an abelian group by a subgroup.
The direct sum \(\bigoplus_{i \in I} A_i\) and direct product \(\prod_{i \in I} A_i\) of any family of abelian groups.

concepts.title: algebraic geometry
concepts.inline: Algebraic geometry is the study of geometric objects defined by polynomial equations, especially varieties and schemes.

concepts.title: algebraic number theory
concepts.inline: Algebraic number theory studies number-theoretic questions using rings of integers in number fields and related algebraic structures.

concepts.title: polynomial rings
concepts.inline: A polynomial ring \(R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\) is the commutative ring of polynomials in \(n\) indeterminates with coefficients in a ring \(R\).

concepts.title: initial object
concepts.inline: An initial object in a category is an object with a unique morphism to every other object.

concepts.title: category of commutative rings
concepts.inline: The category of commutative rings has commutative rings as objects and ring homomorphisms as morphisms.

concepts.title: terminal object
concepts.inline: A terminal object in a category is an object to which every other object has a unique morphism.

concepts.title: Group
concepts.inline: A \emph{group} is a set \(G\) equipped with an associative binary operation, an identity element, and inverses for every element. Groups formalize the algebraic structure underlying symmetry and invertible transformations.

blocks.label: Motivation
blocks.body: Many mathematical structures, from the symmetries of a geometric object to the invertible elements of a ring, share a common pattern: a composition law that is associative, possesses a neutral element, and admits inverses. Isolating these three axioms produces the notion of a group, the most basic algebraic structure capable of expressing reversible operations. Groups appear pervasively in commutative algebra — as the additive structure underlying every ring, as the multiplicative group of units of a ring, and as the Galois groups acting on field extensions — and provide the foundation upon which richer structures such as rings and modules are built.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.body:
A group is a pair \((G, \cdot)\) consisting of a set \(G\) together with a binary operation \(\cdot \colon G \times G \to G\), written \((a, b) \mapsto a \cdot b\), satisfying the following axioms:
(i) Associativity: for all \(a, b, c \in G\), \((a \cdot b) \cdot c = a \cdot (b \cdot c)\).
(ii) Identity: there exists an element \(e \in G\) such that for every \(a \in G\), \(e \cdot a = a \cdot e = a\).
(iii) Inverses: for every \(a \in G\) there exists an element \(a^{-1} \in G\) such that \(a \cdot a^{-1} = a^{-1} \cdot a = e\).
When the operation additionally satisfies \(a \cdot b = b \cdot a\) for all \(a, b \in G\), the group is called abelian.

blocks.label: Proposition
blocks.body: In any group \((G, \cdot)\), the identity element is unique, and each element has a unique inverse. Moreover, the cancellation laws hold: if \(a \cdot b = a \cdot c\) or \(b \cdot a = c \cdot a\), then \(b = c\).
blocks.proof:
Suppose \(e\) and \(e'\) both satisfy the identity axiom. Then \(e = e \cdot e' = e'\), where the first equality uses that \(e'\) is an identity and the second that \(e\) is an identity. Hence the identity element is unique.

Fix \(a \in G\) and suppose \(b\) and \(b'\) are both inverses of \(a\), so that \(a \cdot b = b \cdot a = e\) and \(a \cdot b' = b' \cdot a = e\). Using associativity,
\[ b = b \cdot e = b \cdot (a \cdot b') = (b \cdot a) \cdot b' = e \cdot b' = b', \]
so the inverse of \(a\) is unique.

For the cancellation law, suppose \(a \cdot b = a \cdot c\). Multiplying both sides on the left by \(a^{-1}\) and using associativity together with \(a^{-1} \cdot a = e\) yields
\[ b = e \cdot b = (a^{-1} \cdot a) \cdot b = a^{-1} \cdot (a \cdot b) = a^{-1} \cdot (a \cdot c) = (a^{-1} \cdot a) \cdot c = e \cdot c = c. \]
The right cancellation law is proved analogously by multiplying on the right by \(a^{-1}\).

blocks.label: Examples
items: The integers \((\mathbb{Z}, +)\) form an abelian group with identity \(0\) and inverse \(-n\) of \(n\). The same holds for \((\mathbb{Q}, +)\), \((\mathbb{R}, +)\), and \((\mathbb{C}, +)\).

For any field \(k\), the nonzero elements \(k^{\times} = k \setminus \{0\}\) form an abelian group under multiplication. More generally, for any ring \(R\), the set of units \(R^{\times}\) forms a group under multiplication.
The symmetric group \(S_n\), consisting of all bijections of \(\{1, \dots, n\}\) under composition, is a group; it is non-abelian for \(n \geq 3\).
For each positive integer \(n\), the set \(\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}\) of residues modulo \(n\) is a finite abelian group under addition, and is the prototypical example of a cyclic group.
For any commutative ring \(R\), the underlying additive structure \((R, +)\) is an abelian group; this is part of the definition of a ring.

concepts.title: Ring
concepts.inline: A \emph{ring} is a set equipped with two operations — addition and multiplication — such that addition makes it an abelian group, multiplication is associative with an identity, and the two operations are linked by distributivity.

blocks.label: Motivation
blocks.body: Working with the integers, one quickly notices that addition and multiplication are not independent phenomena: they are bound together by the distributive law \(a(b+c)=ab+ac\), and this single identity is what makes nearly every computation possible. The same intertwining appears in polynomials, in square matrices, in continuous functions on a space, and in the endomorphisms of an abelian group. Each of these systems has its own additive structure (an abelian group) and its own multiplicative structure (an associative operation with identity), and in every case the two interact in exactly the same way. Rather than reprove the same lemmas in each example, one isolates the shared axioms and studies them once. The resulting object is the ring.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.body:
A ring is a triple \((R, +, \cdot)\) consisting of a set \(R\) together with two binary operations \(+\colon R\times R\to R\) and \(\cdot\colon R\times R\to R\) satisfying the following axioms:
(i) \((R,+)\) is an abelian group, with identity element denoted \(0\);
(ii) multiplication is associative: \((a\cdot b)\cdot c = a\cdot(b\cdot c)\) for all \(a,b,c\in R\);
(iii) there exists a multiplicative identity \(1\in R\) such that \(1\cdot a = a\cdot 1 = a\) for all \(a\in R\);
(iv) multiplication distributes over addition on both sides: \(a\cdot(b+c) = a\cdot b + a\cdot c\) and \((a+b)\cdot c = a\cdot c + b\cdot c\) for all \(a,b,c\in R\).
The ring is called commutative if in addition \(a\cdot b = b\cdot a\) for all \(a,b\in R\).

blocks.label: Proposition
blocks.body: In any ring \(R\), the element \(0\) is absorbing for multiplication, i.e. \(0\cdot a = a\cdot 0 = 0\) for all \(a\in R\); moreover \((-1)\cdot a = -a\), and the multiplicative identity \(1\) is unique.
blocks.proof: Let \(a\in R\). Using distributivity and the fact that \(0\) is the additive identity, we have \[0\cdot a = (0+0)\cdot a = 0\cdot a + 0\cdot a.\] Adding \(-(0\cdot a)\) to both sides yields \(0 = 0\cdot a\). The argument on the other side is symmetric, giving \(a\cdot 0 = 0\). Next, since \(1 + (-1) = 0\), distributivity gives \[a + (-1)\cdot a = 1\cdot a + (-1)\cdot a = (1 + (-1))\cdot a = 0\cdot a = 0,\] so \((-1)\cdot a\) is the additive inverse of \(a\), i.e. \((-1)\cdot a = -a\). Finally, if \(1'\) is another element satisfying \(1'\cdot a = a\cdot 1' = a\) for all \(a\), then \(1 = 1\cdot 1' = 1'\), so the multiplicative identity is unique.

blocks.label: Examples
items: The integers \(\mathbb{Z}\) form a commutative ring; this is the prototypical example.
For any ring \(R\), the polynomial ring \(R[x]\) is again a ring, commutative whenever \(R\) is.
The set \(M_n(R)\) of \(n\times n\) matrices with entries in a ring \(R\) is a ring under matrix addition and multiplication; for \(n\geq 2\) it is non-commutative even when \(R\) is commutative.
For any abelian group \(A\), the set \(\mathrm{End}(A)\) of group homomorphisms \(A\to A\) forms a ring under pointwise addition and composition.
The zero ring \(R = \{0\}\), in which \(0 = 1\), is the unique ring with one element; every other ring satisfies \(0\neq 1\).

concepts.title: homomorphisms
concepts.inline: A group homomorphism is a map between groups that preserves the group operation.

concepts.title: homological algebra
concepts.inline: Homological algebra is the branch of algebra studying chain complexes, derived functors, and (co)homology in abelian categories.

concepts.title: category of abelian groups
concepts.inline: The category of abelian groups is the category whose objects are abelian groups and whose morphisms are group homomorphisms.

concepts.title: abelian category
concepts.inline: An abelian category is an additive category in which every morphism has a kernel and cokernel and every monomorphism (resp. epimorphism) is a kernel (resp. cokernel).

concepts.title: cyclic groups
concepts.inline: A cyclic group is a group generated by a single element.

concepts.title: direct sum
concepts.inline: The direct sum \(\bigoplus_{i \in I} A_i\) of a family of abelian groups is the subgroup of the direct product consisting of tuples with only finitely many nonzero entries.

concepts.title: direct product
concepts.inline: The direct product \(\prod_{i \in I} A_i\) of a family of groups is the Cartesian product equipped with componentwise operation.

concepts.title: Galois groups
concepts.inline: A Galois group is the group of field automorphisms of a field extension fixing the base field.

concepts.title: field extensions
concepts.inline: A field extension is a pair of fields \(k \subseteq K\) with \(K\) containing \(k\) as a subfield.
Reduced rings are rings containing no non-zero nilpotent elements.

concepts.title: images
concepts.inline: The image of a ring homomorphism \(\varphi: R \to S\) is the subring \(\varphi(R) \subseteq S\).

concepts.title: zero divisors
concepts.inline: A zero divisor in a ring is a nonzero element \(a\) such that \(ab = 0\) for some nonzero \(b\).

concepts.title: zero ideal
concepts.inline: The zero ideal of a ring \(R\) is the ideal \(\{0\}\), often denoted \((0)\).

concepts.title: Gaussian integers
concepts.inline: The Gaussian integers are the ring \(\mathbb{Z}[i] = \{a + bi : a, b \in \mathbb{Z}\}\), a subring of \(\mathbb{C}\).

concepts.title: Coprime Ideals
concepts.inline: Two ideals \(\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b}\) of a commutative ring \(R\) are coprime (or comaximal) when \(\mathfrak{a}+\mathfrak{b}=R\). This generalizes the notion of two integers having no common prime factor and underlies the Chinese Remainder Theorem.

blocks.label: Motivation
blocks.body: In the integers, two numbers like \(8\) and \(15\) share no common factor, and this lets us solve simultaneous congruences: any pair of remainders modulo \(8\) and modulo \(15\) can be realized by a single integer. But what is it about \(8\) and \(15\) that makes this work? Writing \(\gcd(8,15)=1\) hides the real mechanism, which is the Bézout identity \(2\cdot 8 - 1\cdot 15 = 1\): the number \(1\) lives in the set of all combinations \(8\mathbb{Z}+15\mathbb{Z}\). In a general commutative ring there may be no notion of greatest common divisor, yet the sum of two ideals always makes sense. The condition that this sum recover the whole ring is exactly the structural fact we need, and once isolated it makes the splitting of quotients feel inevitable.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.body: Let \(R\) be a commutative ring and let \(\mathfrak{a},\mathfrak{b}\subseteq R\) be ideals. We say \(\mathfrak{a}\) and \(\mathfrak{b}\) are coprime (equivalently comaximal) if their sum is the whole ring, that is \[ \mathfrak{a}+\mathfrak{b}=R. \]

blocks.label: Equivalent Characterizations
items: There exist elements \(a\in\mathfrak{a}\) and \(b\in\mathfrak{b}\) with \(a+b=1\).
No maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{m}\) of \(R\) contains both \(\mathfrak{a}\) and \(\mathfrak{b}\).
blocks.proof: Since \(\mathfrak{a}+\mathfrak{b}\) is an ideal of \(R\), it equals \(R\) if and only if it contains the unit \(1\), because an ideal containing a unit is all of \(R\). But \(1\in\mathfrak{a}+\mathfrak{b}\) means precisely that \(1=a+b\) for some \(a\in\mathfrak{a}\) and \(b\in\mathfrak{b}\); this gives the equivalence with the first characterization. For the second, suppose \(\mathfrak{a}+\mathfrak{b}=R\) and that some maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{m}\) contained both \(\mathfrak{a}\) and \(\mathfrak{b}\). Then \(\mathfrak{m}\supseteq\mathfrak{a}+\mathfrak{b}=R\), contradicting that \(\mathfrak{m}\) is proper. Conversely, suppose \(\mathfrak{a}+\mathfrak{b}\neq R\). Then \(\mathfrak{a}+\mathfrak{b}\) is a proper ideal, and every proper ideal is contained in some maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{m}\) by an application of Zorn's lemma. This \(\mathfrak{m}\) contains \(\mathfrak{a}+\mathfrak{b}\) and hence both \(\mathfrak{a}\) and \(\mathfrak{b}\), so the second condition fails. Thus the negations correspond, proving the equivalence.

blocks.label: Proposition
blocks.body: If \(\mathfrak{a}\) and \(\mathfrak{b}\) are coprime, then \(\mathfrak{a}\cap\mathfrak{b}=\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}\), and the natural map induces an isomorphism of rings \[ R/(\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b})\;\cong\;R/\mathfrak{a}\,\times\,R/\mathfrak{b}. \] This is the Chinese Remainder Theorem.
blocks.proof: The inclusion \(\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}\subseteq\mathfrak{a}\cap\mathfrak{b}\) holds for any two ideals, since every generator \(ab\) with \(a\in\mathfrak{a}\), \(b\in\mathfrak{b}\) lies in both \(\mathfrak{a}\) and \(\mathfrak{b}\). For the reverse inclusion we use coprimality: choose \(a\in\mathfrak{a}\) and \(b\in\mathfrak{b}\) with \(a+b=1\). Given \(x\in\mathfrak{a}\cap\mathfrak{b}\), multiply the identity by \(x\) to obtain \[ x = x\cdot 1 = xa + xb. \] Here \(xb\in\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}\) because \(x\in\mathfrak{a}\) and \(b\in\mathfrak{b}\), while \(xa\in\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}\) because \(a\in\mathfrak{a}\) and \(x\in\mathfrak{b}\). Hence \(x\in\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}\), proving \(\mathfrak{a}\cap\mathfrak{b}=\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}\). Now consider the ring homomorphism \[ \varphi:R\longrightarrow R/\mathfrak{a}\times R/\mathfrak{b},\qquad \varphi(r)=(r+\mathfrak{a},\,r+\mathfrak{b}). \] Its kernel is \(\mathfrak{a}\cap\mathfrak{b}=\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b}\). To see that \(\varphi\) is surjective, take any target element \((u+\mathfrak{a},\,v+\mathfrak{b})\). Using \(a+b=1\) with \(a\equiv 0\pmod{\mathfrak{a}}\), \(a\equiv 1\pmod{\mathfrak{b}}\) and symmetrically \(b\equiv 1\pmod{\mathfrak{a}}\), \(b\equiv 0\pmod{\mathfrak{b}}\), set \(r = ub + va\). Then \(r\equiv u\cdot 1 + v\cdot 0 = u \pmod{\mathfrak{a}}\) and \(r\equiv u\cdot 0 + v\cdot 1 = v \pmod{\mathfrak{b}}\), so \(\varphi(r)=(u+\mathfrak{a},\,v+\mathfrak{b})\). By the first isomorphism theorem, \(\varphi\) descends to an isomorphism \(R/(\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b})\cong R/\mathfrak{a}\times R/\mathfrak{b}\).

blocks.label: Examples
items: In \(\mathbb{Z}\), the principal ideals \((m)\) and \((n)\) are coprime exactly when \(\gcd(m,n)=1\); for instance \((8)+(15)=\mathbb{Z}\) because \(2\cdot 8 - 15 = 1\), recovering the classical Chinese Remainder Theorem \(\mathbb{Z}/120\cong\mathbb{Z}/8\times\mathbb{Z}/15\).
In the polynomial ring \(k[x]\) over a field, the ideals \((x-a)\) and \((x-b)\) are coprime whenever \(a\neq b\), since \(\frac{1}{b-a}\big((x-a)-(x-b)\big)=1\).
Two distinct maximal ideals \(\mathfrak{m}_1\neq\mathfrak{m}_2\) are always coprime: their sum strictly contains \(\mathfrak{m}_1\), so by maximality \(\mathfrak{m}_1+\mathfrak{m}_2=R\).
The ideals \((2)\) and \((4)\) in \(\mathbb{Z}\) are not coprime, since \((2)+(4)=(2)\neq\mathbb{Z}\); both lie inside the maximal ideal \((2)\).

concepts.title: Chinese Remainder Theorem
concepts.inline: The Chinese Remainder Theorem states that if ideals \(\mathfrak{a}\) and \(\mathfrak{b}\) are coprime, then \(R/(\mathfrak{a}\mathfrak{b})\cong R/\mathfrak{a}\times R/\mathfrak{b}\).

concepts.title: isomorphism of rings
concepts.inline: A ring isomorphism is a bijective ring homomorphism whose inverse is also a ring homomorphism.
